claims.text: Interface coherency controls progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers.
Sharp, coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission across layers.
Easier dislocation transmission at sharp interfaces causes earlier plasticity.
Easier dislocation transmission at sharp interfaces produces higher creep rates.
Diffuse, semi-coherent interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion at diffuse interfaces delays plastic yielding.
Impeded dislocation motion at diffuse interfaces reduces creep rates.
The initial material is a nanoscale CoCrFeMnNi multilayer containing engineered FCC and BCC layers.
Standard deposition conditions produce inherently sharp interfaces in the proposed baseline.
Controlled deposition and post-deposition annealing can create sharp-interface and diffuse-interface sample sets while retaining the same bulk composition.
Testing at approximately 0.3–0.5 Tm enables dislocation activity while preserving the multilayer architecture.
Interface coherency mediates dislocation nucleation and transmission across the layers.
Dislocations accumulate and pile up at interfaces under sustained load.
Interfacial misfit and structural complexity in diffuse interfaces hinder dislocation transmission.
Relative to sharp-interface samples, diffuse-interface samples will have a delayed onset of plastic deformation and lower creep rates.
Substantial changes in layer thickness, temperature outside 0.3–0.5 Tm, or bulk composition could obscure the interface effect.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order may independently influence dislocation dynamics.
